body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Predicting prolonged emergency department boarding at the time of the admission decision: development and external validation of a logistic model","authors":"Osei-Whitfield R, Brandt-Nakamura E, Delgado-Hughes P","year":2019,"venue":"Emergency Care Operations Research","doi":"10.5555/ecor.2019.0133","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We developed a logistic model predicting boarding of more than four hours from nine predictors available at the admission decision, including hour, weekday, admitting service and inpatient occupancy, using 48,200 admissions at one hospital, and validated it at a second hospital. Discrimination fell from a c statistic of 0.78 in development to 0.71 in validation. Calibration was poor in the validation hospital, where 58 percent of patients boarded more than four hours against a mean predicted risk of 44 percent. Recalibration of the intercept corrected most of the difference. The authors advise local recalibration before any model is used."},{"title":"External validation of a commercial boarding prediction tool in three hospitals","authors":"Kowalewski-Adeyemi T, Lindgren-Soto M, Haddad-Pereira N","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Hospital Flow Management","doi":"10.5555/jhfm.2023.0208","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We validated a commercial boarding prediction tool in 61,400 admission decisions at three hospitals that did not contribute to its development. At the vendor's recommended threshold, sensitivity for boarding of four hours or more was 0.62 (95 percent CI 0.60 to 0.64) and specificity 0.71 (95 percent CI 0.70 to 0.72). Sensitivity was 0.49 for admission decisions made at night and 0.66 during the day. Calibration differed between hospitals and was worst in the busiest one. The tool's own published validation had used only its development sites."},{"title":"A hospital command centre and emergency department boarding: an interrupted time series","authors":"Grieve-Mensah L, Okafor-Stroud B","year":2022,"venue":"Hospital Operations Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/hoq.2022.0071","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A 600-bed hospital opened a patient flow command centre with a live display of flagged admitted patients. In an interrupted time series over 36 months, mean boarding hours per admitted patient fell from 6.2 to 5.4 after the opening, with no change in the pre-existing trend. The study did not assess the accuracy of the flags that directed the command centre's work, and a new discharge lounge opened three months later. The authors could not say which parts of the command centre produced the change."},{"title":"Occupancy, not patient characteristics, drives emergency department boarding time: a multilevel analysis","authors":"Ferreira-Nwosu D, Hallberg-Kaur S","year":2015,"venue":"Emergency Care Operations Research","doi":"10.5555/ecor.2015.0044","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 27,900 admissions over two years, inpatient occupancy at the hour of the admission decision explained most of the variation in boarding time between days. Adding patient characteristics to a model with occupancy and time of day raised the c statistic only from 0.74 to 0.76. Boarding over four hours occurred on 81 percent of days when occupancy exceeded 92 percent. The authors suggest that tools flagging individual patients mostly identify busy days rather than patients who need escalation, and that occupancy should be the comparison for any patient-level score."},{"title":"Spectrum effects in predicting hospital bed waits: accuracy by admitting service and time of day","authors":"Rasmussen-Obi A, Castellanos-Tran J","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Hospital Flow Management","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined the accuracy of a bed wait prediction score across patient groups in 19,300 admission decisions. At a fixed threshold, sensitivity for waits of four hours or more was 0.68 for medical admissions and 0.51 for surgical admissions, and specificity was higher for surgical admissions. Accuracy was lowest for admissions decided between midnight and 06:00. Reporting a single overall sensitivity hid these differences. The authors recommend reporting accuracy separately by admitting service and time of day in any evaluation of such scores."},{"title":"Reference standards for boarding time: agreement between emergency department timestamps and bed management records","authors":"Achterberg-Mwangi P, Sorensen-Lee K","year":2020,"venue":"Health Information Quality","doi":"10.5555/hiq.2020.0118","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared emergency department departure timestamps with bed management records and direct observation for 2,400 admitted patients. The departure timestamp was recorded on average 22 minutes after the patient physically left, and 7 percent of admissions had no departure time. Near the four-hour threshold, these delays misclassified about 5 percent of patients as prolonged boarders. Using the bed management arrival time on the ward as a check reduced misclassification. The authors recommend a documented reference standard with a rule for missing times."}]}
